title: “I Didn’t Expect Jenin Could Change So Much”: Reporter Jailed for Nearly 2 Years on Israel’s Destruction
author: Guest Contributor DSN
content:
_Palestinian journalist and Drop Site contributor Mujahed Al-Saadi was born
and raised in the Jenin refugee camp. A seasoned reporter, he has covered the
occupied West Bank since 2012, focusing on Jenin and the surrounding areas._

_In September 2024, he was violently arrested by Israeli authorities from his
home and thrown into prison where he was held for nearly two years in
administrative detention without charge or trial. You can read his account of
his brutal imprisonment[here](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/palestinian-
journalist-israeli-megiddo-prison-jenin-mujahed-saadi)._

_During Al-Saadi 's 22 months behind bars, Jenin underwent a violent
transformation. The Israeli military launched a massive military operation
targeting the Jenin, Tulkarem, and Nur Shams refugee camps in the northern
West Bank, displacing over 30,000 people in the single largest displacement of
Palestinians in the territory since 1967._

_After his release in July 2026, Al-Saadi returned to Jenin to find not only
his hometown devastated but his ability to work as a journalist almost
impossible._

_In this dispatch, Al-Saadi recounts the changes to his work and to Jenin,
particularly the destruction of the camp, from the perspective of someone who
was locked up and prevented from witnessing it as it was unfolding, and
instead was forced to contend with the entirety of the transformation all at
once._

_-- Sharif Abdel Kouddous_

_Story by Mujahed Al-Saadi_

JENIN, occupied West Bank--I didn't expect Jenin could change so much in the
22 months I was locked up in the occupation's prisons. When I returned after
my release in July, it was as if an earthquake had struck the entire area--not
only had the Jenin refugee camp been destroyed, emptied, and occupied, but the
landscape of journalism had entirely shifted.

The first time I went back into the field to report, it was overwhelming.
There was a different kind of pressure, with the sheer volume of the news and
the struggle to verify it, and the difficulty of reaching places the
occupation had targeted.

Over the years, I have worked for several local and international news
organisations covering different parts of the occupied West Bank, but these
past few months have been the most difficult I've experienced as a journalist
working in the field for over a decade.

When I donned my press vest for the first time after nearly two years, I had
been away from reporting, or even being aware of the news, during one of the
most difficult and consequential periods since the occupation of Palestine
began.

I would say that working as a journalist in the West Bank today, particularly
reporting from the northern cities like Jenin, has become one of the most
dangerous jobs in the world.

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd0fa130e-c8d9-4423-874b-0f30157e21b8_1280x960.jpeg)Mujahed
Al-Saadi reporting from Jenin on September 8, 2024, less than two weeks before
his arrest by Israeli forces. Photo courtesy of Mujahed Al-Saadi.

Jenin governorate, where I primarily work, is now carved up into several areas
that are divided and difficult to reach because of newly established
checkpoints and the construction of new settlements and outposts. Some 14
settlements and Israeli military camps have been established in the towns
surrounding the city of Jenin, and trying to access the scenes of incidents
has become an ordeal, particularly with the frequent road closures. At these
checkpoints, in addition to checking identification documents, people's phones
and social media accounts are inspected. Journalistic equipment is frequently
destroyed, confiscated, or stolen.

Conditions on the ground in this area have always been extremely dangerous,
but since I returned to work, it's clear the risks have increased
significantly. The occupation is tightening its grip more and more. Troops
open fire without any justification, detain journalists for hours, prevent
them from moving freely, and subject them to interrogation.

We also have to be careful about every word we write or every image we publish
online. Even just writing about settlements, for example, or the history of
Palestine can make you a target of Israeli security forces. This is what has
changed over the past two years--it was still risky before, but there was
greater freedom to report and express opinions.

Just accessing information has become almost impossible and relaying it
dangerous. Reaching the places targeted by the occupation, such as bedouin and
rural communities around Jenin and the people whose stories we try to tell, is
difficult with all the closures. It is then a risk simply to share information
or detail the repeated attacks against them. A journalist can even be detained
simply for having certain media in their possession, let alone for publishing
it.

Two years ago, I could work and move around the governorate relatively
normally. Today, if I want to write an article or film a story about the
plight of the Jenin refugee camp, for example, and the people that once called
it home, I may need more than two days just to coordinate with those families,
who have been displaced to villages surrounding the city, with occupation
forces stationed between these villages and in some neighborhoods on the
outskirts of the city.

Jenin--both the city and the refugee camp within it--have been transformed.
The city is no longer the "Mother of Gardens," as it was once known. The
refugee camp, a tight-knit community of families who had lived there for
decades, has been emptied, its residents scattered, once again facing
displacement, homelessness, and oppression.

The city and the camp had already been living through a particularly harsh
security situation in the years before, with repeated Israeli incursions,
armed clashes, and systematic damage to roads and civilian infrastructure. At
the same time, internal tensions with the Palestinian Authority (PA) were
escalating. On December 5, 2024, the PA launched a large-scale [military
campaign](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/palestinian-authority-west-bank-
jenin-assault) in Jenin dubbed "Operation Homeland Protection," which it
claimed was to maintain security and establish the rule of law. The
devastating campaign continued until January 21, 2025.

The entire governorate was affected, and the local economy was hit hard. In
July 2024, the Palestinian Ministry of Economy reported that some 53% of
companies and businesses in the governorate had been affected amid a sharp
decline in demand and production capacity. Some were forced to shut down
completely, others partially.

But the biggest turning point came on January 21, 2025, just hours after PA
forces withdrew from the camp, when Israeli forces launched a massive assault
on the camp, which later expanded to the Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps.
"Operation Iron Wall" forcibly displaced 33,000 Palestinians from their homes
in the three camps and destroyed or severely damaged homes, roads, water and
sewage systems, telecommunication networks, and other civilian infrastructure.
The basic necessities of life were no longer there. Israeli forces remain in
the camps and have prevented residents from returning.

The security situation inside Jenin camp used to be shaped by the presence of
multiple armed groups, tensions between the PA and these factions, and
repeated Israeli military operations. When I returned to Jenin, the entire
security equation had completely changed.

In 2024, despite the damage and destruction caused by repeated Israeli
incursions, the camp was still alive and densely crowded with residents
spilling out of streets, alleyways, homes, and public gathering places. By
2026, the camp was empty--large parts of its landscape had been transformed by
bulldozing, home demolitions, the construction of new roads, and the removal
of entire sections of the built environment. At night, the camp is now a patch
of darkness surrounded by the other lit areas of the city--a swathe of land
emptied of life.

Over 600 days of displacement have taken a heavy toll on the camp's former
residents: their hearts have grown old, their bodies have aged, and economic
hardship has exhausted them. The camp has been changed, and the people who
once lived there have too.

But the changes are not limited to the camp itself. An Israeli military base
and observation post has been established in the Al-Jabriyat neighborhood in
the heart of the city, an area classified as Area A under the Oslo Accords
that technically should fall under full control of the PA. Occupation forces
deployed throughout the city have turned Jenin upside down.

The economy has been devastated. The camp, once an integral part of the city's
economic and social fabric, has been cut off. Movement restrictions have
disrupted access to workplaces, markets, and agricultural land, while the loss
of income has left affected families increasingly dependent on humanitarian
aid that arrives only intermittently.

During the two years of my imprisonment it wasn't just the security and
economy of Jenin refugee camp that had changed, but the very place itself. A
crowded camp where conflict once erupted between multiple parties has become
an empty landscape with traces of war and displacement in its streets, homes,
and infrastructure. The camp is no longer what it once was, and neither are
we.
